passage:
“I should be the team leader,” Anand said. “I've done three inter-school quizzes.”

“You also talk over everyone,” said Tanuja.

“That's not the point.”

“It is the point, Anand. Last time you took credit for my science answer.”

“I said ‘we’ answered it!”

“You said ‘I’.”

Sunita, at the end of the bench, looked at her shoes. Kabir mumbled, “Can we just get on with practice?”

“No,” said Tanuja. “I'm tired of reading the questions while you decide the answers.”

Anand paused. “I... didn't realise it felt like that. I just want people to know I worked hard.”

“Then say ‘we’ in front of the teacher,” said Tanuja. “And let me lead the science round.”

qa.q: How many inter-school quizzes had Anand done?
qa.a: Anand had done three inter-school quizzes.

qa.q: What was Anand really wanting in demanding to be the leader?
qa.a: Anand wanted recognition for the hard work, and underneath the demand was a wish for respect.

qa.q: What did Tanuja ask Anand to do at the end?
qa.a: Tanuja asked Anand to say “we” in front of the teacher and let Tanuja lead the science round.

qa.q: How might Sunita feel sitting at the end of the bench looking at her shoes?
qa.a: Sunita probably feels uncomfortable and unsure whether to speak, wishing the argument would end.

grounding: Teenagers on a team clash over who leads and who gets credit, and the fight is about respect and recognition more than the task.

passage:
I'm Pradeep, and in Class 9 our robotics team nearly fell apart over who would present. Deepak had built the base, I had written the code, and Karan had designed the arm. The night before the fair, Deepak said, “I'll present. It's my robot.” I said, “It's our robot, and my code makes it move.” We shouted for ten minutes about a two-minute speech. Karan sat between us saying nothing.

Looking back, I don't think it was about the speech. I wanted the teacher to see that I mattered. Deepak, I now think, wanted the same. In the end our teacher split the presentation into three parts, and that took the air out of the fight.

qa.q: Who had built the base?
qa.a: Deepak had built the base.

qa.q: What was Pradeep really feeling behind the shouting?
qa.a: Pradeep felt insecure and wanted the teacher to see that Pradeep mattered, so the fight was about recognition more than the speech.

qa.q: What choice by the teacher ended the fight?
qa.a: The teacher split the presentation into three parts so each person spoke.

qa.q: What might Karan have felt sitting silently between the two?
qa.a: Karan probably felt uncomfortable and overlooked, unsure whether to side with anyone, while the arm design was not mentioned.

grounding: Teenagers on a team clash over who presents and who gets credit, and looking back the fight was about respect and recognition.

passage:
The science fair at the district school in Satara was a week away, and Lokesh and Nirmala weren't speaking.
It had started with the water filter. Lokesh wanted sand layers. Nirmala wanted charcoal. The argument got louder every day, until the third member, Bablu, started eating lunch elsewhere.
Their teacher, Mr Patil, sat them down. “Is this about sand or charcoal?”
Lokesh said, “She always gets her way. Last year's project, she presented and everyone said Nirmala's project.”
Nirmala went quiet. “And you never say anything good about my ideas. Just ‘no’.”
Mr Patil nodded. “So it's not about filters.”
They built the filter with both. Lokesh presented the build, Nirmala the testing.

qa.q: How many days away was the science fair?
qa.a: A week away.

qa.q: What was Lokesh really upset about?
qa.a: Lokesh felt resentful and overlooked, because last year everyone called it Nirmala's project.

qa.q: How did Mr Patil help them see the real problem?
qa.a: He asked if it was about sand or charcoal, which let them admit it was about credit and respect.

qa.q: How might Bablu have felt as the fight grew louder?
qa.a: Bablu likely felt uncomfortable and left out, which is why Bablu started eating lunch elsewhere.

grounding: Shows two teenagers clashing over whose idea wins, until they see the fight is really about recognition and respect.

passage:
The robotics team at their school in Toronto had two weeks before the regional competition, and Bao and Rafael were fighting about everything: the arm design, the code, who would drive the robot.
One afternoon, Bao threw down his notebook. “You always act like the leader!”
Rafael shouted back, “Because you never let anyone else decide anything!”
Ms Patel, their coach, waited until they'd both stopped. “When did either of you last say something good about the other's work?”
Silence. Then Bao muttered, “His code is better than mine.” Rafael looked up, surprised. “Your arm design is the best in the region.”
They split it: Bao on the arm, Rafael on the code, and they took turns driving.

qa.q: How long before the regional competition?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What did Bao seem to feel when he threw down his notebook?
qa.a: He felt angry and unrecognised, frustrated that Rafael acted like the leader.

qa.q: What did Ms Patel's question change?
qa.a: It made them name what they admired in each other's work, which showed the fight was about respect, and let them split the roles.

qa.q: How might Rafael have felt when Bao praised his code?
qa.a: He looked surprised and was probably pleased, feeling respected for the first time in weeks.

grounding: Shows teenagers clashing over leadership and credit, until they see the fight is about respect and recognition, not the robot.

passage:
In the robotics lab after school, the argument started over the presentation slides and soon wasn't about slides at all.
"I'm presenting," Raghav said. "I wrote the code."
"And I built the arm," Nandini said. "Last time you presented, you said 'my robot' six times."
Kiran and Tushar exchanged looks and kept soldering.
"That's not..." Raghav stopped. "Fine. You present, then."
"I don't even want to present," Nandini said, her voice cracking. "I want you to say 'we'."
The lab went quiet except for the fan. Raghav looked at the arm she'd built, the neat wiring, the tiny labels.
"Okay," he said slowly. "We split it. You do the build, I do the code. And I'll say 'we'."
Tushar let out a breath. "Great. Now can someone hold this wire?"

qa.q: How many times did Raghav say "my robot" last time?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What does Nandini's voice cracking reveal?
qa.a: Nandini felt hurt and unrecognised; the fight was really about wanting her work acknowledged, not about presenting.

qa.q: What helped settle the fight?
qa.a: Nandini named the real issue, and Raghav looked at her work and agreed to share the stage and say "we".

qa.q: How did Tushar experience the argument?
qa.a: Tushar felt tense and awkward, keeping his head down, and relieved when it ended.

grounding: Shows teenagers on a team clashing over who presents, where the fight is really about credit and recognition.
